title: Comparison of perioperative single-dose antibiotic prophylaxis with a prolonged antibiotic regimen in trauma patients of oral and maxillofacial surgery – a prospective, randomised study on postoperative complications
summary:
An accident can break the jaw or another bone in the face. Such fractures often need surgery. Many bacteria live in the mouth. This is quite normal. During surgery these bacteria get into the wound, and the wound can become inflamed. To prevent this, patients receive a medicine during surgery that kills bacteria. There is good evidence that this medicine helps during surgery.

However, it is unclear whether the medicine has to be given for several more days after surgery. Many hospitals do this. But there is no good evidence for it. Taking the medicine for a long time can cause side effects, for example diarrhoea, nausea or a skin rash. In addition, bacteria can get used to such medicines. The medicines then no longer work. Such bacteria are dangerous for everyone.

We therefore want to know: is a single dose during surgery just as safe as giving the medicine for several days?

To find out, we compare two approaches that are both already used in hospitals. With the first approach, participants receive the medicine only once, during surgery. With the second approach, they continue to receive it for several days afterwards. Chance decides who receives which approach. A total of 440 people are to take part. We then look at how often the wound becomes inflamed during the first eight weeks after surgery and compare the two groups. For this we use the information that is recorded during treatment anyway. There are no additional appointments or examinations.

It may turn out that the single dose is just as safe. In that case, many people would need fewer medicines in future and would have fewer side effects.
conditions: Postoperative surgical site infections as a complication of the surgical treatment of traumatic fractures of the facial skeleton.

interventions.name: Intervention group (group A): Perioperative single-dose antibiotic prophylaxis with ampicillin/sulbactam, or clindamycin in case of known penicillin allergy. Single intravenous administration perioperatively on the day of surgery. No continuation of antibiotic administration after surgery.

Control group (group B): Prolonged antibiotic prophylaxis according to institutional standard (ampicillin/sulbactam, or clindamycin in case of known penicillin allergy). First perioperative administration on the day of surgery. Duration and route of administration of the continued prophylaxis depend

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Surgical treatment of a trauma in the field of oral and maxillofacial surgery at the University Hospital Frankfurt am Main. Capacity to consent, sufficient German language skills to fully understand the written and oral study information, and written informed consent given.
Exclusion criteria:
Exclusion criteria are age under 18 years, lack of capacity to consent or withdrawal or absence of written informed consent, insufficient German language skills to understand the study information, known pregnancy (assessed by medical history) and breastfeeding, known allergy or contraindication to both study substances (ampicillin/sulbactam and clindamycin), immunosuppression or immunodeficiency, pre-existing infection at the trauma or fracture site or manifest signs of infection on admission, systemic antibiotic therapy for another indication at the time of surgery, an injury pattern that is expected to require prolonged antibiotic administration beyond the study protocol, isolated soft tissue injuries without fracture or without exposure of the mucosa, maxillary sinus or paranasal sinuses, severe and otherwise uncontrolled renal or hepatic insufficiency requiring a dose adjustment deviating from the protocol, concurrent participation in another interventional clinical trial, and lack of availability for the planned follow-up.
